answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Where the 40 per cent came from, and how far the figure moves if it changes

questions.onCorrect: A figure that barely moves under any reasonable rate is one we can lean on, and one that swings with the rate is not.

misconceptions.feedback: The multiplication is right, and checking it tells us nothing about whether 40 per cent is. The figure is only as firm as the death rate behind it.
More digits would make the figure look more precise without making it more accurate. What decides its accuracy is the assumed death rate.

choices.label: Whether 4,000 times 0.4 really is 1,600
Why the figure is not given to more digits
Where the 40 per cent came from, and how far the figure moves if it changes

questions.prompt: Hus attacked church practice before printing, and his movement stayed largely in Bohemia. Luther wrote sixty-odd years after Gutenberg, and his writings spread from town to town within weeks. What does this pattern show on its own?
hints: How many different stories would fit these two cases?
Does a difference between two cases tell you what kind of factor made it?

acceptedIdeas: That printing may have mattered, but the pattern alone cannot say how
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That printing may have mattered, but the pattern alone cannot say how

questions.onCorrect: A pattern raises the question, and the terms on the next screens are a way to answer it.

misconceptions.feedback: Two cases fit several stories. Printing might have been a cause, or a condition that widened an audience, and telling those apart needs more than the dates.
The pattern points the other way: the movement that had print spread widely and the one without it did not, so print may well have mattered.

choices.label: That printing may have mattered, but the pattern alone cannot say how
That printing caused the Reformation, since Luther's writings spread so fast
That printing played no part, since reform ideas existed before it

questions.prompt: Gibbon published his first volume in 1776 and Ward-Perkins his book in 2005, and both wrote about the end of the Roman West. What is the gap of more than two centuries most likely to have changed?
hints: Do the three authors disagree about 476?
What kind of evidence did Ward-Perkins argue from?

acceptedIdeas: The questions historians ask and the kinds of evidence they use
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The questions historians ask and the kinds of evidence they use

questions.onCorrect: Ward-Perkins's pottery and coins are one example of evidence a later age brought to an old question.

misconceptions.feedback: The three authors do not quarrel about 476 or the basic facts of the period. Their disagreement lies elsewhere.
Ward-Perkins argued largely from archaeology, and Gibbon worked from written sources, so the two did not start from the same material.

choices.label: Nothing, since both authors worked from the same written sources
The basic facts of the period, which the later book corrects
The questions historians ask and the kinds of evidence they use

questions.prompt: Edward I confirmed Magna Carta in 1297, and in the 1620s lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke cited it against the Stuart kings. What do these later events tell a historian about?
hints: Which time does each piece of evidence come from?
Were the lawyers of the 1620s reporting what the barons meant?

acceptedIdeas: What later people made of the charter, as part of its history
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: What later people made of the charter, as part of its history

questions.onCorrect: The story of those later uses is what historians call the document's afterlife.

misconceptions.feedback: The lawyers of the 1620s read the old text for their own purposes, and some of what they found was not what the barons had meant. For 1215 we need evidence from 1215.
The quarrel of 1215 was decided in 1215: the pope annulled the charter in August and the war went on. Events decades and centuries later answer a different question.

choices.label: What the barons themselves meant by the charter in 1215
Whether the charter settled the quarrel of 1215 for good
What later people made of the charter, as part of its history

questions.prompt: Almost all the surviving written records of the Haitian Revolution were made by people who held power or command. Whose voices would an account built only on them leave mostly unheard?
hints: Who made up most of the colony's people?
Ask who had the chance to learn to read and write.

acceptedIdeas: The enslaved, who made up most of the colony
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The enslaved, who made up most of the colony

questions.onCorrect: Their words reach us mostly when someone else wrote them down, in lists, reports and notices.

misconceptions.feedback: Colonial officials wrote a great deal, and their reports are part of the large body that survives. Losing control of the colony did not remove them from the record.
The planters are among the best-recorded people of the revolution, through their letters and notices. Losing their estates did not silence them in the record.

choices.label: The French officials, who lost control of the colony
The French planters, who lost their estates
The enslaved, who made up most of the colony

questions.prompt: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, a month after the assassination at Sarajevo. How is that declaration best sorted?
hints: When did it act: over years, or during the crisis?
Was it a pressure, a spark or a choice?

acceptedIdeas: A short-term cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short-term cause

questions.onCorrect: It was a choice, and choices made in July 1914 could have gone the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: Long-term causes built up over years, such as the alliances and the arms race. This declaration was a decision taken during the crisis.
The trigger was the shooting at Sarajevo, the event that set the crisis off. The declaration came a month later, as a choice made in response to it.
Conditions are background that makes an outcome possible. A declaration of war is a decision taken during the crisis that moved events along, which is a different kind of factor.

choices.label: A long-term cause
A condition that made a war possible
The trigger
A short-term cause

questions.prompt: Darby smelted iron with coke in 1709, and Watt patented his separate condenser in 1769. Before anyone says what each one shows, what do dated developments like these give a claim about why Britain industrialised early?
hints: What can a date tell you without any further argument?
What would you have to add to turn a dated development into evidence?

acceptedIdeas: Order and spacing, which limit the claim but do not yet support it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Order and spacing, which limit the claim but do not yet support it

questions.onCorrect: The next step is to say what each development shows about coal or wages, and to set aside the ones that bear on neither.

misconceptions.feedback: Counter-evidence points against a claim, and nothing in these two dates does. They tell us what came first and how far apart, and we have not yet said what either shows about coal or wages.
A list of dates does not say why anything happened. To count as evidence for the claim, each development has to be shown to bear on the price of coal or the level of wages.

choices.label: Order and spacing, which limit the claim but do not yet support it
Proof that cheap coal and high wages caused the change
Counter-evidence, since the developments came so long apart

questions.prompt: Luther's Theses of 1517 and the outbreak of war in 1914 are nearly four centuries apart. What do the explanations of the two events have in common?
hints: Think of the terms used for the Reformation and for 1914.
Did the two events share causes, or a way of sorting causes?

acceptedIdeas: The same sorting of factors by kind and by time, ending with a trigger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same sorting of factors by kind and by time, ending with a trigger

questions.onCorrect: A question asked across cases in this way is what we call a thread.

misconceptions.feedback: The two events had different causes: indulgences, print and princes in one, alliances, armies and the decisions of July in the other. What they share is the way the causes were sorted.
Distance in time does not stop us comparing how two events are explained. Both were explained by sorting factors by what kind of thing each was and when it acted.

choices.label: Nothing, since cases that far apart cannot be compared
The same sorting of factors by kind and by time, ending with a trigger
The same causes, since religious conflict led to the war

questions.prompt: The decree praises Ptolemy V for the gifts he gave to Egypt's temples. A historian wants to use the stone as evidence about those gifts. What can the stone show by itself?
hints: Ask whose voice the decree is in.
A text can report a gift without that settling whether the gift was given.

acceptedIdeas: That the priests chose to credit the king with those gifts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the priests chose to credit the king with those gifts

questions.onCorrect: The stone gives us the priests' claim and the reason they made it. Whether the king did what they say is a separate question, and it needs a source made by someone else.

choices.label: That the king gave every gift the decree lists
That the priests chose to credit the king with those gifts
Nothing, since a text that praises its king cannot be evidence

misconceptions.feedback: The decree is the priests' account of the gifts, and a text cannot check its own praise. Whether the king gave them would need a source with no reason to praise him.
Praise limits what the stone can prove, but it does not empty the stone of value. The decree is still the priests' own words, and that is evidence of something.

questions.prompt: A researcher studies how schoolbooks of the 1950s described the Romans, and uses a 1952 textbook on Roman history as her evidence. What kind of source is the textbook for her question?
hints: Ask which period her question is about.
Ask whether the textbook belongs to that period.

acceptedIdeas: A primary source, since it comes from the 1950s she is studying
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A primary source, since it comes from the 1950s she is studying

questions.onCorrect: The textbook now belongs to the time being studied, so it is primary for this question. A label belongs to a question and not to an object.

choices.label: Not a source, since a textbook only repeats what other books say
A secondary source, since it was written long after the Romans
A primary source, since it comes from the 1950s she is studying

misconceptions.feedback: A source is anything people made that a historian puts a question to. A textbook can answer questions about the people who wrote it and used it.
It would be secondary for a question about the Romans. The label belongs to the question, and her question is about something else.

questions.prompt: A historian wants to know what the farmers of Egypt thought of Ptolemy V. How good a source is the decree on the Rosetta Stone for that question?
hints: Ask who is speaking in the decree.
Ask whether the people the question is about had any part in making it.

acceptedIdeas: Little evidence, since the farmers had no part in making it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Little evidence, since the farmers had no part in making it

questions.onCorrect: The decree is the priests' voice. For a question about the farmers it is a primary source that has almost nothing to say, so other evidence is needed.

choices.label: Good evidence, since it is a primary source made at the time
Good evidence, since the priests spoke for all of Egypt
Poor evidence, since copying it onto stone made it a later account
Little evidence, since the farmers had no part in making it

misconceptions.feedback: Primary tells us when the decree was made, not whose views it holds. For this question we need to ask who is speaking in it.
The priests were a small group with their own aims, and nothing in the decree shows that they spoke for the farmers.
Cutting a text on stone does not make it a later account. The priests made the text at the time, so the stone is no less a primary source.

questions.prompt: Augustus died in 14 CE. Suetonius wrote his lives of the Caesars, which include a life of Augustus, about 120 CE, a date we take as a round working figure. How many years apart are they?
hints: Both dates are CE.
Subtract the earlier date from the later.
Work out 120 minus 14.
questions.onCorrect: A gap of 106 years puts Suetonius more than a century after Augustus, so he could not have known him.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dates. The gap is a difference, so subtract.

questions.prompt: The only surviving account of a siege was written by the besiegers, and it says nothing about hunger inside the walls. What follows about hunger in the city?
hints: Ask what the writers could have seen.
Ask what the silence is a silence of.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing certain, since the besiegers could not see inside the walls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing certain, since the besiegers could not see inside the walls

questions.onCorrect: A silence in a source made from outside the walls has several possible causes, so it supports no certain conclusion about the hunger inside.

choices.label: There was no hunger, since the account would have mentioned it
The besiegers hid it, since a siege account would not admit it
Nothing certain, since the besiegers could not see inside the walls

misconceptions.feedback: An account written from outside the walls may simply not have seen the hunger. A silence is not evidence that nothing happened.
A silence may be a choice, but it may also be ignorance or loss. Nothing in the account shows that the besiegers chose to leave hunger out.

questions.prompt: Some historians end the ancient world in 476. Would a person living in Italy in 476 have described that year as the end of the ancient world?
hints: Ask who invented the names of periods.
Ask whether the people living then would have had the later label.

acceptedIdeas: No, since the division into ancient and medieval was made by later scholars
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since the division into ancient and medieval was made by later scholars

questions.onCorrect: The name came later, from scholars who looked back on the centuries between antiquity and their own time.

choices.label: Yes, since the deposition of the western emperor plainly ended an age
No, since the division into ancient and medieval was made by later scholars

misconceptions.feedback: The deposition was a real event, but ancient world is a name that later scholars gave to a stretch of time.

questions.prompt: A survey records 2,500 households in a town, and historians assume between 4 and 6 people per household. How wide is the range of the town's population, from the low estimate to the high one?
hints: Work out the population at 4 per household and at 6 per household.
Subtract the low end from the high end.
Subtract 10,000 from 15,000.
questions.onCorrect: Two extra people per household across 2,500 households add 5,000 people, so the assumption alone moves the answer by that much.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two ends. The width of a range is a difference.
That is the number of households. The two assumptions differ by two people in each, so the range is wider.

hints: Which part of the figure was assumed, and which part was worked out?

acceptedIdeas: Where the 20 per cent came from, and what a different rate would give
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Where the 20 per cent came from, and what a different rate would give

questions.onCorrect: A total that barely moves under any reasonable rate is one we can lean on, and one that swings with the rate is not.

choices.label: Whether 12,000 multiplied by 0.2 really does come to 2,400
Why the total is not given more exactly, to the last person
Where the 20 per cent came from, and what a different rate would give

misconceptions.feedback: The multiplication is easy to check and tells us nothing about the death rate, which is the part that was assumed.
More exact digits would make the total look more precise without making it more accurate. What decides its accuracy lies behind the digits.

questions.prompt: A town's militia list of 1590 names every man aged 16 to 60 who could be called up to fight. Which question can it answer best?
hints: What was the record made to count?
Pick the question that matches what the list names.

acceptedIdeas: How many men the town could call up to fight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many men the town could call up to fight

questions.onCorrect: A record answers best the question it was made for.

choices.label: How many people lived in the town
How many families in the town owned land
How many people in the town died of disease
How many men the town could call up to fight

misconceptions.feedback: The list names men of fighting age only, so a figure for the whole population needs a further assumption about everyone else.
A militia list does not record who owned land. That is a question for a different record, such as a tax survey.

questions.prompt: A harsh new tax was introduced in a town in March. Through the following months the merchants organised a refusal to pay, which spread from street to street. Ask whether it went on for months or happened at one moment.

acceptedIdeas: A cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A cause

choices.label: A cause
A trigger
A condition

misconceptions.feedback: The trigger was the single event that set the revolt off on the day it began. The refusal had been spreading for months.

questions.prompt: Droughts had struck a region many times without causing a famine. In 1840 the region had another drought, and a famine followed that could not have happened without it. What is the best conclusion about the 1840 drought?
hints: Ask what else must have been present in 1840 that was missing in the earlier droughts.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It was necessary but not enough, since other factors had to be present too

questions.onCorrect: A factor can be necessary without being enough. The drought was needed for the famine, and the earlier droughts show that it did not bring one on its own.

choices.label: It was the whole cause, since the famine could not have happened without it
It was not a cause at all, since the earlier droughts brought no famine
It was necessary but not enough, since other factors had to be present too

misconceptions.feedback: If the drought alone had been enough, the earlier droughts would have brought famine as well. Something else was present in 1840.
The famine could not have happened without the drought, so it did matter. The earlier droughts show only that it did not act alone.

questions.prompt: Hus was burned in 1415 and Luther stood before the Diet of Worms in 1521. How many years later was Worms?
hints: Both years are CE.
Subtract the earlier year from the later.
questions.onCorrect: Worms came 106 years after Hus was burned, a span of more than a century.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two years. A gap is a difference, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Two historians agree on every fact about a rebellion. One explains it by new taxes, and her reading fits the timing of each outbreak. The other explains it by religion, and his reading fits none of the dates. Does the disagreement mean that the two readings are equally good?

Ask which reading covers more of the evidence.

acceptedIdeas: No, since the reading that fits more of the evidence is the stronger one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since the reading that fits more of the evidence is the stronger one

questions.onCorrect: A stronger interpretation covers more of the evidence and deals better with what does not fit.

choices.label: Yes, since an interpretation can never be shown right or wrong by evidence
Yes, since both historians begin from exactly the same set of facts
No, since the reading that fits more of the evidence is the stronger one

misconceptions.feedback: Interpretations cannot be proved in one stroke, but they can be compared by how much of the evidence each one covers.
Starting from the same facts does not make two readings equal. What matters is how well each one handles those facts.

questions.prompt: Magna Carta was cited by lawyers for centuries, yet the worked answer calls its significance small for this question. Why?
hints: Ask what question the example fixed in its first line.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because significance is measured against the question, and this one is about 1215

questions.onCorrect: Significance belongs to a question. The charter did little for the dispute of 1215 and a great deal for the lawyers who cited it centuries later.

choices.label: Because significance is measured against the question, and this one is about 1215
Because the lawyers of the 1620s misread it, so their use does not count
Because a charter that lasted ten weeks cannot matter to any question

misconceptions.feedback: The lawyers' use of the charter is real history, and it counts for any question that asks about it. It answers a different question from the one this example fixed at the start.
How long a charter lasted does not decide how much it mattered. The same charter counts for a great deal when the question is about the lawyers of the 1620s.

questions.prompt: A historian asks what the barons wanted from King John in 1215. Which of these is the best evidence?
hints: Ask which of these was made in 1215.
Ask which evidence comes from the barons' own time.

acceptedIdeas: The charter John sealed at Runnymede in 1215
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The charter John sealed at Runnymede in 1215

questions.onCorrect: Evidence about 1215 has to come from 1215. The later uses are real history, but they answer a different question.

choices.label: The charter John sealed at Runnymede in 1215
Sir Edward Coke's use of the charter in the 1620s
Edward I's confirmation of the charter in 1297
The Petition of Right, which cited the charter in 1628

misconceptions.feedback: Coke read the old charter for the purposes of his own day, so his use is evidence about the 1620s.
Edward I confirmed the charter generations later, so his act shows what it was taken to mean in 1297.
The Petition of Right appeals to the charter in 1628, which shows how it was used then and not what the barons wanted.

questions.prompt: An official reports that enslaved people were meeting at night on the estates without their owners' leave. Besides the warning he meant to give, what does his report show?
hints: Ask what the official did not intend to tell his superiors.
Ask who decided that the meetings should take place.

acceptedIdeas: That the people arranged the meetings themselves, at some risk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the people arranged the meetings themselves, at some risk

questions.onCorrect: The report shows people who met and organised by their own decision, although its author meant only to warn his superiors.

choices.label: Nothing about the people, since an official wrote it
That the people arranged the meetings themselves, at some risk
That the official understood the people's reasons for meeting

misconceptions.feedback: A source made by the powerful can still show what others did. Discarding the report throws that away.
The official was asking for stricter policing, so nothing in the report suggests that he understood or shared their reasons.

questions.prompt: A planter writes to his agent that the workers on three estates have stopped work and gone up into the hills together. His letter is best used to learn:
hints: What can the letter show that its author did not intend?
Which option uses the letter for what it can show?

acceptedIdeas: That the workers acted together, though he meant only to report a loss
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the workers acted together, though he meant only to report a loss

questions.onCorrect: A source made by the powerful can still show the actions of others, if we read it for more than its author meant.

choices.label: How the workers explained their reasons, in their own words
Nothing about the workers, since a planter wrote the letter
That the workers acted together, though he meant only to report a loss
That the planter understood why the workers had gone

misconceptions.feedback: The letter is the planter's voice, so it does not give the workers' own words.
A planter's letter is poor evidence of the workers' words, but it is good evidence of what they did. Discarding it throws that away.
The letter reports a loss and gives no sign that the planter knew the workers' reasons.

questions.prompt: On 30 July 1914, two days after Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia ordered its army to mobilise. How is that order best sorted among the causes of the war?
hints: When did it act: over years, or during the crisis?
Was it a pressure, a spark or a choice?

acceptedIdeas: A short-term cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short-term cause

questions.onCorrect: It was a choice, and choices made in July 1914 could have gone the other way.

choices.label: A condition that made a war possible
A short-term cause
The trigger
A long-term cause

misconceptions.feedback: Conditions are background that makes an outcome possible. An order to mobilise is a decision taken during the crisis that moved events along, which is a different kind of factor.
The trigger was the shooting at Sarajevo, the event that set the crisis off. The mobilisation came a month later, as a choice made in response.
Long-term causes built up over years, such as the alliances and the arms race. This order was given during the crisis, two days after a declaration of war.

questions.prompt: How many days are there from 28 June to 3 August 1914, the day Germany declared war on France?
hints: 2 days are left in June after the 28th.
Add all of July and the first 3 days of August.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty-six days passed between the shooting and Germany's declaration of war on France.

misconceptions.feedback: Recount the months: June leaves 2 days, July has 31, August counts to the 3rd.
That runs on to the 4th. The count stops on the 3rd, when Germany declared war on France.

questions.prompt: A historian finds one town where machines were adopted although wages were low, which cuts against her claim about high wages. What is the best way to deal with it?
hints: Has the claim faced the evidence?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Report the town, and qualify the claim to say where it may not hold

questions.onCorrect: A claim that faces its counter-evidence and says where it may not hold is stronger than one that has been protected from it.

choices.label: Leave the town out, since one case cannot overturn a claim
Report the town, and qualify the claim to say where it may not hold
Drop the claim, since one contrary case shows it is false

misconceptions.feedback: A claim that has avoided its counter-evidence has only been protected from it. A reader who finds the town will trust the claim less.
One contrary case counts against a claim that says 'mainly', but it does not by itself settle that the claim is false. It shows what the claim has to account for.

questions.prompt: Watt patented his separate condenser in 1769 and the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825. How many years lie between them?
hints: Both years are CE.
Subtract the earlier from the later.
questions.onCorrect: The railway opened 56 years after Watt's patent.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two years. A gap is a difference, so subtract.
That is the gap from 1712 to 1769. The railway opened in 1825, and the count starts from Watt's patent.

questions.prompt: Which is the best historical claim about why the Reformation spread so quickly through German towns?
hints: Which claim names factors and says how they worked?
Which could be shown wrong?

acceptedIdeas: It spread quickly mainly because printers sold pamphlets cheaply and rulers sheltered Luther
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It spread quickly mainly because printers sold pamphlets cheaply and rulers sheltered Luther

questions.onCorrect: A good claim is specific and qualified, so evidence can count for or against it.

choices.label: It spread quickly for many reasons, and historians weigh them differently
It spread quickly because of print, politics, religion, trade, ideas and luck
It spread quickly mainly because printers sold pamphlets cheaply and rulers sheltered Luther
It spread quickly because it was unstoppable once the Theses had been written

misconceptions.feedback: This is too broad to be wrong, so it tells us nothing.
A list of everything is as safe as the broad claim. It does not say how the factors worked or which mattered.
Inevitable is a claim that no evidence could test, and it overlooks choices and chances.

questions.prompt: Almost everything that survives about Marathon and the Persian Wars was written by Greeks. What does that mean for how a historian reads it?
hints: Think about what survives from the Persian side.
Ask what a historian can set the Greek account beside.

acceptedIdeas: It is one side's telling, with no Persian narrative to set beside it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is one side's telling, with no Persian narrative to set beside it

questions.onCorrect: A story told by one side has to be read as that side's telling, and the missing Persian account is part of the evidence.

choices.label: It can be taken as it stands, since the Greeks were closest to events
It cannot be used, since the winners always rewrite their own history
It is one side's telling, with no Persian narrative to set beside it

misconceptions.feedback: Being close to events is a reason to take a source seriously, not to take it at face value. Herodotus had aims of his own, and no Persian account survives to check him.
The idea that the winners write history is too simple. Survival depends on who could write, what was kept and what was copied, so the account is partial and still usable.

questions.prompt: How many years are there from 196 BCE, the year of the Rosetta decree, to 1914 CE?
hints: The dates lie on opposite sides of the boundary.

flashcards.front: What do we call a source made at the time being studied, or by someone who took part in it?
flashcards.back: A primary source, which stands close to the events, though it can still be one-sided or wrong.

acceptedIdeas: primary source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: primary source

flashcards.front: Explain in a sentence why the same 2020 book can be secondary for one question and primary for another.
flashcards.back: The label depends on the question: the book is a later account of Ptolemaic Egypt, but it is itself part of the time being studied when the question is about 2020s writing.

flashcards.front: In which year (BCE) was the decree on the Rosetta Stone issued?
flashcards.back: 196 BCE, at Memphis, in the name of Ptolemy V.

flashcards.front: What are the four sourcing questions about a text?
flashcards.back: Who made it, when, for whom and why; the answers tell us what the text is best evidence of.

flashcards.front: Name the strengthening of a claim when independent sources agree.
flashcards.back: Corroboration, which needs separate routes to the event, so a copy does not count.

acceptedIdeas: corroboration
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: corroboration

flashcards.front: In what year CE did Augustus die?
flashcards.back: 14 CE, after which the Res Gestae was displayed on bronze pillars in Rome.

flashcards.front: Explain what it means to ask what a silence is a silence of.
flashcards.back: A gap may come from loss, from no record ever made, or from a record not yet read, so it is not proof that nothing happened.

flashcards.front: What do we call a source on the other side of a conflict from its subject?
flashcards.back: A hostile source: it may know what its own side did and still have reason to bend what it says of the other.

acceptedIdeas: hostile source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hostile source

flashcards.front: In which year BCE was the battle of Marathon fought?
flashcards.back: 490 BCE, ten years before Thermopylae and Salamis.

flashcards.front: How many years are there from 1 BCE to 1 CE?
flashcards.back: One year, because there is no year 0 between them.

flashcards.front: Explain how to compute the years from 44 BCE to 14 CE.
flashcards.back: Add the two year numbers and take off one for the missing year 0: 44 + 14 − 1 = 57.

flashcards.front: What number is the century that contains the year 1453?
flashcards.back: The 15th century, which runs from 1401 to 1500.

flashcards.front: What do we call a record of one thing used to stand in for something we cannot count directly?
flashcards.back: A proxy, such as vacant clergy posts standing in for deaths, which covers only part of the population.

acceptedIdeas: proxy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: proxy

flashcards.front: Explain why a count of households does not give a number of people directly.
flashcards.back: A household held several people, so we multiply by an assumed size and report the result as a range.

flashcards.front: A survey records 1,200 households. How many people at 4 per household?
flashcards.back: 1,200 times 4 is 4,800, the low end of the range.

flashcards.front: What do we call the particular event that sets an outcome off once the background is in place?
flashcards.back: A trigger, such as the sale of indulgences in 1517, which worked because the conditions were ready.

acceptedIdeas: trigger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: trigger

flashcards.front: Explain how the counterfactual test works.
flashcards.back: Remove one factor in thought, keep the rest, and ask whether the outcome still seems likely; the answer is a judgement of likelihood.

flashcards.front: In which year did Luther's Ninety-five Theses appear, traditionally?
flashcards.back: 1517, traditionally dated 31 October, though the posting itself is disputed.

flashcards.front: Explain what makes one historical interpretation stronger than another.
flashcards.back: It covers more of the evidence and deals honestly with what does not fit.

flashcards.front: What do we call the study of how history has been written?
flashcards.back: Historiography, which treats earlier historians as evidence of their own time.

acceptedIdeas: historiography
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: historiography

flashcards.front: In which year did Gibbon's first volume appear?
flashcards.back: 1776, the first volume of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.

flashcards.front: Explain in two sentences why Magna Carta matters more now than it did in 1216.
flashcards.back: Its first life was short, but reissues and later uses by lawyers made it a standard reference, so its significance grew with its afterlife.

flashcards.front: What do we call attributing a later idea to an earlier time?
flashcards.back: Anachronism, such as reading a modern bill of rights into a charter for barons.

acceptedIdeas: anachronism
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: anachronism

flashcards.front: On what date was Magna Carta sealed, as a number of the month in June 1215?
flashcards.back: 15 June 1215, at Runnymede.

flashcards.front: What do we call reading a source for what its author did not mean to tell us?
flashcards.back: Reading against the grain, which uses a source for evidence its author never meant to give.

acceptedIdeas: reading against the grain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: reading against the grain

flashcards.front: Explain why a large record can still give a lopsided history.
flashcards.back: A large record can come from only a few groups, such as planters and officials, so it leaves out the voices of people who did not write or were not recorded.

flashcards.front: In which year was Haitian independence declared?
flashcards.back: 1804, on 1 January, after thirteen years of revolution.

flashcards.front: What word names the idea that outcomes depend on choices and chances that could have been otherwise?
flashcards.back: Contingency: it is why a likely war was not necessarily inevitable.

acceptedIdeas: contingency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: contingency

flashcards.front: Name the three layers of causes of the war of 1914 from longest to shortest.
flashcards.back: Long-term causes, short-term causes, and the trigger.

flashcards.front: How many days from 28 June to 4 August 1914?
What do we call evidence that points the other way from a claim?
flashcards.back: Counter-evidence, which a good historian names and deals with.

acceptedIdeas: counter-evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: counter-evidence

flashcards.front: Explain what makes a historical claim narrow enough to be useful.
flashcards.back: It names factors and how they worked, so that some possible evidence would count against it.

flashcards.front: In which year did Newcomen's steam engine come into use pumping water from a mine?
flashcards.back: 1712, at the start of the steam engine's development.

flashcards.front: Name the four sourcing questions, the three kinds of cause and the test for a cause.
flashcards.back: Who made it, when, for whom and why; conditions, causes and a trigger; and the counterfactual test, which asks what would have happened without the factor.

flashcards.front: What do we call a question that we keep asking across several cases?
flashcards.back: A thread, such as who wrote the record.

acceptedIdeas: thread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: thread

flashcards.front: How many years lie between 490 BCE and 1914 CE?
flashcards.back: 490 + 1914 − 1 = 2,403 years, allowing for the missing year 0.
